Cheese goes on in the last minute, after the patty has reached temperature. The residual heat and 30 seconds in the warm basket melt it without extending the cook.

Air fryer hamburger chart: frozen patties

Frozen patties are pre-formed and often pre-seasoned, and they cook evenly from frozen. No thawing and no pressing — pressing squeezes moisture out.

Frozen pattyTemperatureTimeNotes
1/4 lb frozen patty380°F / 193°C12–15 minFlip at halfway
1/3 lb frozen patty380°F / 193°C14–17 minFlip at halfway
1/2 lb frozen patty380°F / 193°C16–19 minCheck at 14 minutes
Thin frozen patties380°F / 193°C10–12 minShake or flip once

Frozen patties frequently need the long end of their range. The center thaws as it cooks, so the thermometer should confirm the middle before you build the burger.

Fat, smoke and the drip tray

Burgers release fat as they cook, and in an air fryer that fat collects under the basket. Two habits keep the smoke down: cook within the chart's temperatures rather than hotter, and empty or wipe the drawer between batches. Adding water to the drip tray — a tablespoon under the basket — also catches spatter and reduces smoke on fatty blends.

An 80/20 blend gives the juiciest result. Leaner beef dries out faster than the chart's shortest time; fattier blends splatter more. Either way, the internal temperature target does not move.

Five mistakes with air fryer burgers

  1. Judging by the crust. A deep-brown outside can hide a raw center; probe the middle every time.
  2. Pressing patties during cooking. Pressing squeezes out the juices that make burgers tender.
  3. Cooking straight from the fridge. Cold centers lag; let patties sit out 15 minutes for even timing.
  4. Overworking the meat. Compact patties turn dense; mix just until the seasoning is spread.
  5. Skipping the dimple. Flat-center patties dome up and cook unevenly at the edges.

Frequently asked questions

How long do burgers take in an air fryer? 8–12 minutes at 380°F / 193°C for fresh quarter- to third-pound patties, flipped halfway; frozen patties need 12–17 minutes. Verify the center reaches 160°F / 71°C.

What temperature do air fryer burgers need inside? 160°F / 71°C — the USDA minimum for all ground beef, fresh or frozen. Use an instant-read thermometer through the side of the patty.

Can I cook a medium-rare burger? Ground beef must reach 160°F / 71°C under USDA rules, which rules out rare and medium-rare. A steak can be cooked lower because its center never touched the surface; ground beef has no such exception.

Do burgers smoke in an air fryer? Some smoke is normal with fatty beef. Keep the temperature at or below 380°F / 193°C, wipe the drawer between batches, and add a spoon of water to the drip tray.

Can I cook burgers and fries together? Not well. Fries need shaking and dry air; burgers release fat. Cook the burgers first, wipe the drawer, then cook fries at 400°F / 205°C.

Burgers in the air fryer are simple once you accept the thermometer. Even patties with a dimple, 380°F / 193°C, a flip at halfway, and 160°F / 71°C in the middle — everything else is garnish.

Always verify doneness with an instant-read thermometer. Cooking times are starting points and vary by appliance model, wattage and basket size.

entry.title: Air Fryer Hard Boiled Eggs (Times by Doneness)
entry.summary: Air fryer hard boiled eggs by doneness, with soft, jammy and hard times, hot start and cold start methods, the ice bath and honest peeling notes.
entry.content:
Air frying eggs is not frying, and it is not boiling. You set whole eggs in the shell in the basket, run the machine low, and take them out with no pot to scrub.

The results are real, and so are the limits. Here are the times by doneness, plus an honest answer on peeling.

Times vary by appliance model — use a thermometer for meat and a timer for eggs. Wattage and basket size move the clock more for eggs than for anything else.

Why people cook eggs in an air fryer

Two reasons: hands-off cooking with no pot of water to heat, and the claim that air fryer eggs peel more easily, which this page deals with below.

The trade is that a shell hides everything: you cannot see the yolk set, and you cannot read the center of an intact egg without breaking it. Time is your only control.

Air fryer egg chart by doneness

Times are for large eggs from the refrigerator, in a single layer, in a basket that was not preheated.

DonenessTemperatureTimeYolk and white
Soft250°F / 121°C8–11 minRunny yolk, white barely set
Soft-medium250°F / 121°C11–13 minThick liquid yolk, set white
Jammy250°F / 121°C13–16 minFudgy, glossy yolk, no run
Hard250°F / 121°C16–19 minFully set yolk, firm white
Very firm260°F / 127°C18–21 minDry, pale yolk that slices

Medium eggs finish 1–2 minutes early and extra-large eggs need 1–2 minutes more. If the shells keep cracking, drop to 240°F / 116°C.

Hot start versus cold start

A cold start puts the eggs in a room-temperature basket and then starts the machine. A hot start preheats for about 3 minutes first. Both work; the choice is about time and cracking.

MethodTemperatureJammyHardWhat changes
Cold start250°F / 121°C13–16 min16–19 minGentler on the shell, more forgiving
Hot start250°F / 121°C11–13 min14–16 minFaster, but shells crack more often

Never stack eggs in two layers, and turn them once at halfway.

Ice bath, then peel

Move the eggs straight from the basket into ice water for 5–10 minutes. The cooking stops instead of coasting, which keeps a jammy yolk jammy, and the egg pulls away from the shell membrane as it cools.

To peel, tap the wide end on the counter until the shell cracks — that is where the air pocket sits. Roll the egg under your palm to craze the shell, then peel from the wide end in a bowl of cold water.

The peeling debate: what is actually proven

Search this topic and you will find confident claims that air fryer eggs peel perfectly every time. Treat them as anecdotal; no controlled comparison against boiled eggs has been published.

What is known about peeling has little to do with the heat source. Very fresh eggs are harder to peel, because the white holds more carbon dioxide and the membrane clings. You will still get a torn egg now and then, so a chart that promises a perfect peel every time is describing luck.

What the air fryer does not do better than boiling

Boiling is not a worse method, just a different one, and in several ways it is the better tool:

  • Volume. A basket holds 6–8 large eggs in one layer. A pot holds 12 or more.
  • Evenness. Water surrounds each egg at one temperature. Moving air does not, so doneness varies.
  • Repeatability. Boiling has a timeline you learn once. Air fryer timing shifts with wattage and basket size.

The air fryer wins the small batch: 2–6 eggs, no stove, no waiting for a boil.

Egg safety, plainly

USDA lists 160°F / 71°C for egg dishes — custards, quiches, casseroles — and 145°F / 63°C for shell eggs cooked to order for immediate service. Neither is a probe-and-pull instruction for a whole egg, because there is no practical way to read the middle of an intact shell.

So use time and one test egg: crack the smallest first, and add 2 minutes if it is looser than you wanted. Refrigerate what you do not eat within two hours.

Five mistakes with air fryer eggs

  1. Stacking eggs. Two layers means the top eggs cook faster and the bottom ones stay raw.
  2. Skipping the ice bath. Carryover heat keeps cooking the yolk after the basket stops.
  3. Using the hottest setting. The white turns rubbery before the yolk is ready.
  4. Peeling immediately. Give the eggs 5–10 minutes in ice water first, or the white tears.
  5. Judging by the shell. A cracked shell says nothing about the yolk inside.

Frequently asked questions

How long do hard boiled eggs take in an air fryer? 16–19 minutes at 250°F / 121°C from a cold start for large eggs. Check one egg at 16 minutes and add time in 2-minute steps.

Do air fryer eggs really peel easier? Some people report it, but it is anecdotal rather than measured. Egg age, an ice bath and peeling from the wide end matter more than the appliance.

Why is there a green ring around my yolk? That is iron and sulfur from the white reacting at the yolk surface, which means the egg was cooked long or cooled slowly. Pull the eggs 1 minute earlier and use the ice bath.

The short version

Air fryer eggs are a small-batch tool, not a replacement for a pot. Use 250°F / 121°C, give them 8–19 minutes for the yolk you want, turn them once, and ice-bath them the moment they come out.

Always verify doneness with an instant-read thermometer. Cooking times are starting points and vary by appliance model, wattage and basket size.

entry.title: Air Fryer Meal Prep Chart: What Batches Well and What Does Not
entry.summary: Air fryer meal prep that actually holds up: what batches well, what turns to mush, the order to cook in, and the cooling and reheating rules.
entry.content:
An air fryer is a small, fast convection oven, which makes it a surprisingly good batch-cooking tool. It is also a small basket, so "batch" means several rounds, not one heroic load.

The trick is planning the order. Cook in the wrong sequence and something sits raw on the counter while the machine is busy.

Air fryer models differ in wattage, basket size and how close the element sits to the food. Treat every time below as a range, and verify doneness with an instant-read thermometer.

Start with the two rules

Rule one: pull food by temperature, not by the clock. Two air fryers of the same size can differ by several minutes on the same potato.

Rule two: everything waiting its turn goes in the refrigerator. Not on the counter, not on the stovetop. Food that sits out while you cook the next batch is the main way meal prep goes wrong.

What batches well, and what does not

This is the table that saves the most time. Some foods reheat better than they cook the first time; others should never be prepped in advance.

FoodBatches wellWhy
Chicken thighs (boneless)YesReheats to 165°F / 74°C and stays juicy
Chicken breastYes, with careDries out; reheat at a lower temperature
Ground meat and meatballsYesReheats to 160°F / 71°C without toughening
Steak and pork chopsYes, slicedBest slightly underdone, then finished quickly
Potatoes, wedges, cubesYesReheat crisp at 380°F / 193°C
Broccoli, cauliflower, Brussels sproutsYesFirm enough to survive a second pass
Tofu and halloumiYesReheat crisp in 4–6 min
Breaded foods and nuggetsYesOften crisper than the first time
SalmonOnly if eaten coldReheats dry; better flaked into a salad
Shrimp and shellfishNoTurns rubbery fast
RiceNot recommendedNeeds fast cooling and careful handling
Zucchini, peppers, green beansNoRelease water and go soft
Anything in a wet sauceNoCoating slides off in the basket

The one temperature table you need

Keep this next to the air fryer. Every number is a range on purpose.

FoodTemperatureTimeSafe internal temperature
Chicken pieces (bone-in)380°F / 193°C25–30 min165°F / 74°C
Chicken breast (boneless)375°F / 190°C18–22 min165°F / 74°C
Ground meat and meatballs390°F / 199°C10–14 min160°F / 71°C
Sausages380°F / 193°C12–15 min160°F / 71°C
Steak and pork chops400°F / 205°C10–14 min145°F / 63°C + 3 min rest
Salmon fillets390°F / 199°C9–12 min145°F / 63°C
Potato wedges400°F / 205°C18–22 minNot applicable
Broccoli and cauliflower390°F / 199°C10–14 minNot applicable
Carrots and root vegetables380°F / 193°C15–18 minNot applicable

The order to cook in

Cook longest first, and group foods that share a temperature. Raw meat never shares a basket with vegetables you plan to eat cold.

StepWhat goes inTimeWhile it runs
1Potatoes or root vegetables18–22 minChop the next vegetable
2Chicken or other protein18–30 minCool batch one in a shallow container
3Ground meat or meatballs10–14 minPack batch two and refrigerate
4Broccoli or cauliflower10–14 minWipe the basket, set out containers
5Tofu or a second vegetable12–15 minStart cooling the last batch

That is roughly 80–110 min of machine time, counting the preheat between rounds. A two-hour window covers it.

Cooling and refrigerating

Cooling is the part people rush. Hot food sealed in a deep container stays warm for a long time, which is exactly what you do not want.

  1. Portion before you store. Divide big batches into the containers you will eat from.
  2. Go shallow. Spread food out so more surface area is exposed.
  3. Leave the lid off until the steam stops. Cover once it is no longer steaming.
  4. Refrigerate promptly. Do not leave cooked food out while you clean up.

The common guidance for cooked leftovers is 3–4 days in the refrigerator, and about 3–4 months in the freezer. Follow your local food-safety authority if it gives different numbers, and throw out anything that smells or looks off.

Reheat leftovers to 165°F / 74°C, measured in the thickest part — not until it feels warm.

Frequently asked questions

Can I cook raw chicken and vegetables together? No. Raw meat needs its own round, and the basket needs washing before vegetables go back in. Chicken is done at 165°F / 74°C.

How long do meal prep containers last? The common guidance is 3–4 days in the refrigerator for cooked food. After that, the risk is not worth the convenience.

Can I prep a whole week in one session? You can cook it, but a shorter window is safer and tastes better. Cooking for 3–4 days and repeating is the usual compromise.

How do I reheat without drying food out? Use a lower temperature than you cooked at, start with 3–5 min, and check. A splash of water under a loose foil tent helps lean proteins.

Five meal prep mistakes

  1. Treating the air fryer like a full oven. It holds one layer, so plan for rounds.
  2. Reheating by feel. 165°F / 74°C is a number, and a thermometer is the only way to read it.
  3. Lidding hot containers. Trapped steam is how leftovers turn soggy.
  4. Storing everything for the same number of days. Fish and rice are not chicken thighs.
  5. Prepping rice and pasta this way. Both need fast cooling and careful handling, and a stovetop suits them better.

The short version

Batch what holds up: chicken thighs, ground meat, potatoes, firm vegetables, breaded foods. Skip what does not: shrimp, rice, and anything in a wet sauce. Cook longest first, keep everything cold until its turn, cool in shallow containers, and reheat to 165°F / 74°C.

Always verify doneness with an instant-read thermometer. Cooking times are starting points and vary by appliance model, wattage and basket size.

entry.title: Air Fryer Meatballs: Fresh and Frozen Times and Temperatures
entry.summary: Air fryer meatball times for beef, pork, turkey and chicken, fresh or frozen, with the 160°F / 71°C ground meat rule and no medium-rare.
entry.content:
Meatballs are one of the best things an air fryer does: they brown on every side without a pan of oil, they hold their shape if you handle them once, and they freeze and reheat well.

They are also the clearest example of a rule people get wrong: a meatball is ground meat, and ground meat has no medium-rare.

Times vary by appliance model — use a thermometer. Wattage and basket size change the clock, but 160°F / 71°C and 165°F / 74°C do not change.

The rule: ground meat has no medium-rare

A whole steak can be served pink because the bacteria sit on the surface, where heat reaches them first. Grinding mixes that surface through the entire ball. Every part of the meatball is now surface, so the center has to reach the safe temperature. There is no pink middle that is safe by the same standard as a medium-rare steak.

Meatball typeSafe internal temperature
Beef, pork, veal or lamb meatballs160°F / 71°C
Turkey or chicken meatballs165°F / 74°C
Reheated meatball leftovers165°F / 74°C

Ground poultry is treated as poultry, not as ground beef; the gap between 160°F / 71°C and 165°F / 74°C is not a rounding detail. Probe the center of the thickest meatball, then probe a second one, because a batch browns unevenly.

Fresh meatballs: temperature and time

The sizes below are about 1.5 inches across, roughly 1 to 1.5 ounces each. Times assume a preheated basket, a single layer, and a little space between the balls.

Meatball typeTemperatureTimeNotes
Beef, 1.5 inch380°F / 193°C10–14 min160°F / 71°C
Pork, 1.5 inch380°F / 193°C10–14 min160°F / 71°C
Turkey, 1.5 inch380°F / 193°C11–15 min165°F / 74°C
Chicken, 1.5 inch380°F / 193°C11–15 min165°F / 74°C
Mini meatballs, 1 inch390°F / 199°C8–11 minShake at 5 min
Large, 2 inch370°F / 188°C14–18 minCheck at 12 min

Turkey and chicken need a few extra minutes because they are leaner and dry out faster. A lean mix also sticks more, so oil the meatballs, not the basket.

Chill the mix for 15 minutes before shaping; a warm mix slumps into a flat puck, and a puck browns on fewer faces.

Why the basket needs shaking and rolling

A meatball rests on one flat face, and that face browns last. Shake the basket at the halfway mark so the balls roll onto a new side, or turn them with tongs if they are large or sitting close together.

Wait until a crust has set before you touch them, usually about 5 minutes in, or a raw ball smears on the basket floor.

Two layers is the other common failure: the balls underneath get no direct air, so they steam and soften the ones above.

Why meatballs stick

CauseFix
Very lean turkey or chicken mixOil the meatballs lightly before they go in
Cold basketPreheat for 3 minutes at the cooking temperature
No binderAdd one egg and 2–3 tablespoons of breadcrumbs per pound
Balls pressed flatShape with wet hands and a light touch, do not pack them

Cooking meatballs from frozen

Frozen meatballs come in two kinds. Precooked frozen meatballs, the kind sold in a bag, only need heating. Raw frozen meatballs, usually homemade, need to cook through at a lower temperature so the outside does not burn before the center thaws.

Frozen meatballsTemperatureTimeNotes
Precooked, beef or pork390°F / 199°C10–12 min160°F / 71°C
Precooked, chicken or turkey390°F / 199°C10–12 min165°F / 74°C
Raw, homemade, 1.5 inch360°F / 182°C18–24 minCheck at 16 min
Raw, large, 2 inch350°F / 177°C22–28 minLower heat, longer time

Never thaw raw meatballs on the counter; thaw them in the refrigerator, or cook them from frozen using the times above. A raw frozen meatball dropped into a basket at 400°F / 205°C comes out dark outside and cold in the middle.

Five mistakes with air fryer meatballs

  1. Cooking to color instead of temperature. Browning starts long before the center is done.
  2. Looking for a pink middle. There is no safe pink middle in ground meat.
  3. Overcrowding the basket. Two layers steam the bottom row.
  4. Rolling too soon. A raw ball smears; wait for the crust to set.
  5. Using one number for every meat. Beef and pork are 160°F / 71°C; turkey and chicken are 165°F / 74°C.

Frequently asked questions

What temperature do I cook meatballs in an air fryer? 380°F / 193°C for fresh, 390°F / 199°C for precooked frozen. Either way they must reach 160°F / 71°C for beef, pork, veal or lamb, and 165°F / 74°C for turkey or chicken.

Can I cook them from frozen? Yes. Precooked frozen meatballs take 10–12 minutes at 390°F / 199°C. Raw frozen meatballs need 18–24 minutes at 360°F / 182°C so the center catches up with the outside.

Do I need to flip meatballs? A shake at halfway is enough for small ones. For two-inch meatballs, turn each one once with tongs.

Are meatballs done at 145°F / 63°C? No. 145°F / 63°C with a 3-minute rest is the standard for whole cuts of beef and pork, not for ground meat. Ground beef and ground pork are 160°F / 71°C, and ground poultry is 165°F / 74°C.

The short version

Portion evenly, chill the mix, oil the meatballs, preheat the basket, and cook in a single layer at 380°F / 193°C for 10–15 minutes, shaking at halfway. Probe the center: 160°F / 71°C for beef and pork, 165°F / 74°C for turkey and chicken. Precooked frozen: 390°F / 199°C for 10–12 minutes.

Always verify doneness with an instant-read thermometer. Cooking times are starting points and vary by appliance model, wattage and basket size.

entry.title: Air Fryer Meatloaf: Time and Temperature Chart
entry.summary: Air fryer meatloaf times by loaf size, with glaze timing, mini meatloaf settings and the internal temperature ground meat must reach.
entry.content:
Meatloaf is the classic oven dish the air fryer quietly does better: the circulating heat browns the whole surface, the glaze sets instead of steaming, and a weeknight loaf is done in half the time. The catch is that a loaf is dense, and dense ground meat is the easiest thing in the kitchen to undercook in the middle.

This chart covers loaf sizes and glaze timing. Like all ground meat under USDA rules, meatloaf must reach 160°F / 71°C inside — the glaze, the crust and the size of the loaf do not change that.

Times vary by appliance model — use a thermometer. Wattage, basket size and loaf shape change the clock, but 160°F / 71°C does not change.

Air fryer meatloaf chart

Roast meatloaf at a moderate temperature so the center cooks through before the outside hardens. Rest the loaf 5 minutes after cooking so it slices cleanly.

LoafTemperatureTimeNotes
1 lb loaf, free-form350°F / 177°C25–35 minProbe the center
1.5 lb loaf, loaf pan350°F / 177°C35–45 minCheck at 35 min
2 lb loaf, loaf pan350°F / 177°C45–55 minFoil on top if browning fast
Mini meatloaves, 4 oz each375°F / 190°C15–20 minBest shape for the air fryer
Meatloaf muffins, 2 oz each375°F / 190°C12–15 minTwo per batch, no overlap

The probe target is the geometric center of the loaf. Insert the thermometer from the side or the end, horizontally, so the tip sits in the middle of the thickest part. When it reads 160°F / 71°C, the loaf is done everywhere.

Why the air fryer suits meatloaf

An oven heats meatloaf from all sides at once, but the air around the loaf is still — the crust forms slowly and the glaze often steams. The air fryer moves hot air across every surface, so the Maillard browning arrives early and the glaze caramelizes instead of softening.

StageWhat happens
First 15 minutesFat renders into the drip tray; surface begins to brown
Mid-cookGlaze sets; edges pull slightly from the pan
Final minutesThermometer confirms the center; glaze darkens
Rest, 5 minutesJuices settle; slices hold together

Because the air fryer browns faster than an oven, a sugary glaze can go from mahogany to burnt in minutes. Apply half the glaze in the last 10 minutes and the rest after the loaf is out — you get color without char.

Bread crumbs, milk and the binder

The binder is what keeps meatloaf tender instead of dense. Bread crumbs soaked in milk (or any liquid) hold moisture as the loaf cooks and create the soft crumb that defines the dish. A standard ratio is one egg and a quarter cup of liquid-soaked crumbs per pound of meat.

Two practical notes for the air fryer specifically:

  • Loaf pans fit most baskets but block air underneath; free-form loaves cook more evenly.
  • A pan also catches fat. If your basket has no drip clearance, place the loaf on a small rack or a few onion slices so grease drains away from the meat.

Five mistakes with air fryer meatloaf

  1. Trusting the crust color. The outside browns long before the center is done; only a center probe counts.
  2. Cooking at 400°F / 205°C. High heat sets the crust early and leaves the middle behind.
  3. Skipping the rest. Cutting straight from the basket spills the juices and crumbles the slice.
  4. Glazing from the start. Sugary glazes scorch; glaze late in thin layers.
  5. Packing the meat too tight. Compressed meat shrinks hard and cooks unevenly; shape it loosely.

Frequently asked questions

How long does meatloaf take in an air fryer? 25–35 minutes at 350°F / 177°C for a 1 pound loaf, 35–45 minutes for 1.5 pounds, and 45–55 minutes for 2 pounds. Mini meatloaves take 15–20 minutes at 375°F / 190°C.

What temperature should meatloaf be inside? 160°F / 71°C in the center. Meatloaf is ground meat, and USDA rules require that internal temperature regardless of loaf size.

Can I use a loaf pan in the air fryer? Yes, if it fits with air space around it. Metal and silicone pans both work; expect a few extra minutes versus free-form, since the pan shields the bottom.

Why is my meatloaf dry? Too little binder, too long a cook, or very lean meat. Soak the crumbs, verify the center promptly at 160°F / 71°C, and rest the loaf before slicing.

Can I cook meatloaf from frozen? Raw meatloaf should be thawed before cooking — the center must reach 160°F / 71°C, and a frozen loaf browns outside while the middle is still thawing. Cooked slices and reheating leftovers to steaming work fine in the basket.

Meatloaf rewards moderation: moderate heat, a verified center, a rest before slicing. Get the middle to 160°F / 71°C and the air fryer will hand you the best crust this dish has ever had.

Always verify doneness with an instant-read thermometer. Cooking times are starting points and vary by appliance model, wattage and basket size.

entry.title: Air Fryer Mozzarella Sticks: Fresh and Frozen Times
entry.summary: Air fryer mozzarella stick times for frozen and homemade sticks, with the temperature that melts without bursting and the freeze-first rule.
entry.content:
Mozzarella sticks are the snack the air fryer handles better than any deep fryer: less oil, no splatter, and a crisp coating around a molten center. They are also the easiest snack to ruin — two extra minutes and the cheese bursts out of the coating and welds itself to the basket.

This chart covers frozen and homemade sticks, plus the temperature logic that keeps the cheese inside where it belongs.

Times vary by appliance model. Brand size, coating thickness and basket crowding change the clock — watch the first batch and learn your machine.

Air fryer mozzarella sticks chart

Frozen sticks go straight into the basket — no thawing, no oil spray. Thawing softens the coating and guarantees a burst.

StickTemperatureTimeNotes
Frozen, standard (3–4 inch)390°F / 199°C6–9 minFlip at halfway
Frozen, mini390°F / 199°C5–7 minShake once
Frozen, thick bakery-style380°F / 193°C8–10 minLower heat, watch closely
Homemade, breaded and frozen380°F / 193°C8–10 minFreeze 30+ min first
Homemade, breaded fresh380°F / 193°C6–8 minCoating is fragile when wet

Start checking at the low end of the range. The visual cue is subtle: the coating turns deep gold and the first thread of cheese appears at a seam — that is done. Two minutes past that point is a burst.

Why they burst — and the temperature that prevents it

Mozzarella melts fully between 130°F / 54°C and 150°F / 66°C, and keeps liquefying as it climbs. The coating protects the cheese only while it holds its shape. Heat the stick too long and the cheese turns fully liquid, expands, and escapes through any weak seam.

TemperatureWhat happens
370°F / 188°CSlow melt, safest for thick or homemade sticks
390°F / 199°CThe standard: crisp coating, molten center, no burst
400°F / 205°CFast but risky — the cheese can burst before the coating browns

The fix for a burst is always lower-and-shorter, never hotter-and-longer. If your brand bursts at 390°F / 199°C, drop to 380°F / 193°C and shave a minute off the time.

The homemade route

Homemade sticks beat frozen on flavor and cost — with one non-negotiable rule: freeze the breaded sticks for at least 30 minutes before cooking. A wet, room-temperature coating slides off the cheese the moment it melts.

The breading sequence is standard: flour, then beaten egg, then seasoned bread crumbs — repeat the egg and crumbs for a second coat. The double coat is what holds the molten center; a single coat bursts easily.

StepTimeNotes
Cut mozzarella into sticks—Low-moisture, block mozzarella only
Flour, egg, crumbs, egg, crumbs5 minDouble coat holds the melt
Freeze on a tray30+ minNon-negotiable for no-burst
Cook from frozen380°F / 193°C, 8–10 minFlip at halfway

Freeze the whole tray, then bag the sticks for future batches — they cook straight from frozen for months.

Five mistakes with air fryer mozzarella sticks

  1. Thawing frozen sticks. Soft coating plus melting cheese equals a guaranteed burst.
  2. Cooking past the first cheese thread. The moment cheese shows at a seam, they are done.
  3. Single-coating homemade sticks. One coat cannot hold molten cheese; double-coat and freeze.
  4. Skipping the flip. The basket-side coating stays pale and soft without one turn.
  5. Piling them in a second row. Sticks touching weld together as the cheese escapes.

Frequently asked questions

How long do frozen mozzarella sticks take in an air fryer? 6–9 minutes at 390°F / 199°C for standard sticks, flipped at halfway. Mini sticks need 5–7 minutes; thick bakery-style sticks 8–10 minutes at 380°F / 193°C.

Why did my mozzarella sticks explode? They cooked too long or too hot. The cheese liquefies and escapes through the coating's seams. Drop the temperature 10 degrees and shave a minute, and pull them at the first cheese thread.

Do I need oil spray for mozzarella sticks? No. Frozen sticks carry their own coating fat. Homemade sticks get enough from the double coat.

Can I cook homemade sticks without freezing first? The coating will slide off. Thirty minutes in the freezer firms the breading enough to hold — it is the one step that cannot be skipped.

What temperature do I reheat leftover sticks? 350°F / 177°C for 3–4 minutes restores most of the crunch without a second burst.

Mozzarella sticks reward restraint: frozen, 390°F / 199°C, flip once, pull at the first cheese thread. For homemade, double-coat and freeze — the air fryer handles the rest.

Always verify doneness with an instant-read thermometer. Cooking times are starting points and vary by appliance model, wattage and basket size.

entry.title: Air Fryer Appetizers Chart for Parties and Game Day
entry.summary: Air fryer appetizers chart for game day: mozzarella sticks, poppers, pigs in blankets, stuffed mushrooms, garlic bread, dumplings and potato skins.
entry.content:
An air fryer is the best party appliance you own and the worst one to serve from directly. It holds one layer of food, which means a crowd gets served in waves, not at once.

Plan for that. Pick appetizers that hold well, cook in a sensible order, and keep a warm oven ready. The chart below gives you the temperatures and times; the rest of the page is about timing, so nothing arrives cold.

Times vary by appliance model — use a thermometer. Frozen and reheated party food should reach 165°F / 74°C in the centre before you serve it.

Party appetizer chart

Everything here assumes a preheated basket and a single layer. Half a batch in two layers takes longer than the full batch in one, and it cooks unevenly.

AppetizerTemperatureTimeBatch notes
Mozzarella sticks, frozen390°F / 199°C6–9 minDo not thaw, they leak
Jalapeño poppers, frozen or fresh380°F / 193°C9–13 minCut side up, pin bacon with a pick
Chicken wings380°F / 193°C22–26 minOur chicken chart has the full wing method
Pigs in blankets375°F / 190°C10–14 minSeam side down, do not crowd
Stuffed mushrooms370°F / 188°C10–12 minStem side up, filling heaped
Garlic bread, from frozen380°F / 193°C6–9 minButter side up, watch the last minute
Dumplings or potstickers, frozen380°F / 193°C9–13 minBrush with oil, shake at halfway
Potato skins, halved400°F / 205°C8–12 minFilling side up, add cheese late

Every item on that table is a range for a real reason. Two machines with the same wattage can differ by 3 minutes on a basket of mozzarella sticks, depending on how close the element sits to the food.

Cooking in batches without going cold

The order of operations matters more than any single time on this page. Sort your appetizers into three groups: food that holds well, food that must be served hot, and food that takes longest. Then work backwards from the time you want to eat.

OrderGroupCookHold
1Longest cookers, they hold wellChicken wings and potato skins20–25 min in a 200°F / 93°C oven
2Frozen and sturdyMozzarella sticks, poppers, dumplings15–20 min on a tray in the oven
3Quick and delicatePigs in blankets, garlic bread10 min, and they lose crispness after that
4LastAnything you want crispServe immediately, straight from the basket

A warm oven at 200°F / 93°C is the tool that makes this work. Set a baking sheet with a rack in it, and move each finished batch onto the rack as it comes out. The rack matters: a flat tray traps steam under the food and softens the coating within minutes, while a rack lets air reach the underside.

Three practical rules for the sequence:

  • Move in the same direction all night. Finish one batch, tip it out onto the rack, add the next batch to the basket. Do not try to cook two groups at once.
  • Use a timer, not your memory. Each appetizer needs a different clock, and you will be talking to people. Set the timer the moment the basket closes.
  • Do not stack batches on the rack. One layer on the rack, or the bottom layer goes soggy.

Serve sauces in small bowls rather than pouring them over the food. A wet appetizer stops being crisp, and a shared bowl of dip is also a shared surface, so give people a spoon or individual cups.

Left out on the table: the food-safety note

The standard food-safety guidance is simple and it is not optional. Perishable food sitting in the temperature danger zone for hours is where party food causes problems, and the danger zone is roughly 40–140°F / 4–60°C. Cheese, meat, dairy fillings and dips all count as perishable.

So:

  • Keep hot food hot. Hold it at 140°F / 60°C or above in a warm oven, or serve it in small batches you replace as they empty.
  • Refrigerate within two hours. If food has been out longer than that, throw it away rather than reheating it.
  • Reheat to 165°F / 74°C. Any cooked food you reheat, including leftovers from the party, should reach 165°F / 74°C throughout. An air fryer is a good tool for this, but the thermometer is still the check.
Reheated party foodSafe internal temperature
Wings, pigs in blankets, any poultry or pork dish165°F / 74°C
Ground meat fillings, meatballs, sausage stuffing160°F / 71°C
Whole cuts of beef or pork145°F / 63°C + 3 min rest
Fish and shellfish appetizers145°F / 63°C
Any cooked leftovers, reheated165°F / 74°C

If a platter holds a mix, go by the highest number on it. That is usually the poultry.

Five mistakes with party appetizers

  1. Starting with the quick items. Garlic bread is done in 6 minutes and cold in 15. Cook it last.
  2. Two layers to save time. The bottom layer steams, the top layer burns, and both are uneven.
  3. Skipping the rack. Appetizers on a flat tray go soft fast. Use a rack over a sheet pan.
  4. Leaving food out all evening. Two hours is the limit for perishable food, less if the room is warm.
  5. Thawing frozen appetizers first. Mozzarella sticks and dumplings hold their shape best straight from the freezer.

Frequently asked questions

How do I keep air fryer appetizers warm for a party? Hold them in a 200°F / 93°C oven on a rack over a sheet pan. That keeps them hot without cooking them further, and the rack keeps the coating crisp.

How long do mozzarella sticks take in an air fryer? 6–9 min at 390°F / 199°C from frozen, in a single layer. If cheese leaks out, the temperature is too high or they were thawed first.

Can I cook two different appetizers at once? Only if they need the same temperature and roughly the same time. Otherwise cook them in sequence and hold the first batch in the oven.

How long can party food sit out? Two hours for perishable food, and less in a warm room. After that, refrigerate it or throw it away. Reheat anything you keep to 165°F / 74°C.

Can I make potato skins ahead? Yes. Bake them, cool them, and refrigerate. Reheat at 400°F / 205°C for 8–12 min and add the cheese for the last 2 minutes.

The short version

One layer per batch, one timer per batch, and a 200°F / 93°C oven with a rack as your holding station. Cook the long items first and the delicate ones last. Keep perishable food out of the danger zone, refrigerate within two hours, and reheat leftovers to 165°F / 74°C.

Always verify doneness with an instant-read thermometer. Cooking times are starting points and vary by appliance model, wattage and basket size.

entry.title: Air Fryer Pizza Chart (Frozen, Fresh Dough and More)
entry.summary: Air fryer pizza times and temperatures for frozen personal pizza, leftover slices, fresh dough, tortilla, naan and pita bases, with checks for each.
entry.content:
Pizza is one of the best things an air fryer does, as long as you match the base to the basket. A tortilla turns crisp in five minutes. Raw dough in the same basket at the same temperature comes out pale and doughy.

The difference is water and mass. Thin, dry bases lose their moisture fast and brown. Fresh dough carries a lot of water and needs room and time to cook through before the top burns.

Times vary by appliance model — use a thermometer. Frozen pizzas and reheated leftovers should reach 165°F / 74°C in the centre before you eat them.

Air fryer pizza chart by base

All times assume a preheated basket, one pizza at a time, and a base that fits with at least half an inch of clearance on every side.

BaseTemperatureTimeNotes
Frozen personal pizza370–390°F / 188–199°C8–12 minCheck at 8 min, centre 165°F / 74°C
Leftover slices360°F / 182°C3–5 minCrisp base, cheese just melting
Fresh dough, rolled thin350–375°F / 177–190°C7–10 minPart-bake the base for 4–5 min first
Flour tortilla375–400°F / 190–205°C4–6 minWatch it, it scorches fast
Naan or flatbread375°F / 190°C5–7 minThicker base, slightly longer
Pita, split open375°F / 190°C4–6 minSplit side up holds the sauce
English muffin halves380°F / 193°C4–6 minToast cut side down first
French bread or baguette half375°F / 190°C5–8 minHollow it slightly so it does not sag

Add 1–2 minutes if your machine runs cool or you add a heavy load of toppings. Take one minute off if your base is very thin.

Frozen, leftover and raw are three different jobs

Frozen personal pizza. It goes in cold, straight from the freezer, and the centre is the last thing to heat. The crust browns before the middle is hot, which is why the range is wide. Probe the centre of the cheese and sauce, not the crust, and look for 165°F / 74°C. Some thin frozen pizzas finish in 8 minutes; a thick one with dense toppings can take 12.

Leftover slices. This is a short reheat, not a bake. Three to five minutes at 360°F / 182°C brings back the crisp base that a microwave destroys. Put the slice cheese side up, keep it in a single layer, and take it out as soon as the cheese loosens. Reheated leftovers should reach 165°F / 74°C, so if the slice is thick, give it another minute rather than eating it lukewarm. Refrigerate leftover pizza within two hours of cooking and eat it within 3–4 days.

Fresh dough. The one case that genuinely needs a different method. See below.

Why wet dough needs a smaller basket and lower heat

Fresh pizza dough is roughly 60 percent water, and that water has to leave the dough before the base can crisp. In a small basket there is less air volume, so the fan recirculates hot air over a shorter path and the element can sit much closer to the top of the dough. That is a problem: the cheese and the crust surface brown and burn while the inside of the dough is still raw and wet.

Two adjustments fix it:

  • Use a smaller base, not a bigger oven. Roll the dough to a size that leaves clearance around it. A 6-inch round in a 6-quart basket cooks far better than an 8-inch round pressed against the sides, because air has to be able to move around the edge and under the base.
  • Drop the temperature to 350–375°F / 177–190°C. Lower air temperature buys the inside of the dough time to set before the top is dark. If your cheese is browning before the base is firm, drop 25°F / 15°C.

A useful trick is a two-stage bake. Put the rolled dough in alone for 4–5 minutes at 350°F / 177°C, flip it, then add sauce and cheese and finish for another 3–5 minutes. The part-bake firms the base so it can support the toppings.

Toppings control the outcome

ToppingProblemWhat to do
PepperoniReleases a lot of fatPat the top dry at halfway
Raw sausage or chickenNeeds far more time than the crustCook it fully first, to 160°F / 71°C or 165°F / 74°C
Bell peppers, onion, mushroomsWatery, they steam the baseSlice thin and pat dry
Fresh spinachReleases water as it wiltsWilt and squeeze it first
PineappleVery wet, burns at the edgesDrain well and cut small
Extra cheeseWeighs the base downUse less than you think, keep it inside the rim
Cold sauce straight from the fridgeSlows the centreBring it to room temperature first

Five mistakes with air fryer pizza

  1. Not preheating. A cold basket gives you a soggy bottom. Give it 3–5 minutes.
  2. Using a base that touches the sides. Air cannot circulate, so the edge stays pale and the middle cooks unevenly.
  3. Piling on wet toppings. Every watery topping adds steam that keeps the crust soft.
  4. Cooking raw dough at 400°F / 205°C. The top burns before the dough sets. Lower the heat and part-bake the base.
  5. Leaving the pizza in the basket after it is done. The residual heat and trapped steam soften the base within a couple of minutes. Move it to a rack.

Frequently asked questions

Can I cook a frozen pizza in an air fryer? Yes, if it fits flat with clearance around it. Cook at 370–390°F / 188–199°C for 8–12 min and check the centre for 165°F / 74°C. Cut a larger pizza to fit rather than bending it.

How long do you reheat pizza in an air fryer? 3–5 min at 360°F / 182°C for a standard slice. Two slices side by side need 1–2 min more, and they should not overlap.

Can I put raw pizza dough in an air fryer? Yes, rolled thin and no wider than the basket floor. Part-bake the base for 4–5 min at 350°F / 177°C, then add toppings and finish for 3–5 min.

Do I need parchment under pizza? It helps with cleanup on fresh dough, but it must be perforated and weighted down by the dough. A loose liner can lift into the heating element, so never use one you cannot pin under the food.

Is a tortilla pizza the same as a flatbread pizza? Close enough. Both are thin, dry bases that cook in 4–7 min at 375–400°F / 190–205°C. The tortilla is thinner, so it needs the shorter time and more attention.

The short version

Match the base to the job. Frozen personal pizzas take 8–12 min at 370–390°F / 188–199°C. Leftover slices take 3–5 min at 360°F / 182°C. Fresh dough needs a smaller round, lower heat and a part-bake. Thin bases want high heat and your full attention. Verify the centre at 165°F / 74°C and eat it straight away.

Always verify doneness with an instant-read thermometer. Cooking times are starting points and vary by appliance model, wattage and basket size.

entry.title: Air Fryer Pork Chops (Times by Thickness and Cut)
entry.summary: Air fryer pork chops by thickness, bone-in and boneless, with the 145°F / 63°C rule plus a 3 minute rest, brine times and breaded options.
entry.content:
Pork chops are lean, thin and easy to overcook — exactly the profile an air fryer handles badly if you guess. The target is lower than most people expect.

Here is what matters: whole cuts of pork are done at 145°F / 63°C followed by a 3 minute rest, not 165°F / 74°C. Chops cooked to 165°F / 74°C are safe and gray, which is why a lot of people believe they do not like pork.

Times vary by appliance model — use a thermometer. Wattage, basket size and the thickness of the chop change the clock, but 145°F / 63°C plus a 3 minute rest does not change.

The 145°F / 63°C rule and the 3 minute rest

USDA sets 145°F / 63°C for whole cuts of pork — chops, loin, tenderloin and roasts — with a 3 minute rest. The rest is part of the standard: the temperature has to hold for three minutes, and a chop pulled at 145°F / 63°C under foil does that.

Ground pork is a different number: pork sausage and meatballs need 160°F / 71°C, because grinding moves surface bacteria through the whole mass.

Pork and related foodsSafe internal temperature
Pork chops, loin, tenderloin, roasts145°F / 63°C plus a 3 minute rest
Ground pork, pork sausage, meatballs160°F / 71°C
Pork leftovers, reheated165°F / 74°C
Chicken or turkey served alongside165°F / 74°C

Probe the thickest part of the meat, away from bone and fat.

Air fryer pork chop chart by thickness

Times assume a preheated basket, one layer, and chops at refrigerator temperature. Add 2–4 minutes if your model runs cool.

ChopTemperatureTimeNotes
Boneless, 1/2 inch400°F / 205°C7–9 minFlip at 4 min
Boneless, 3/4 inch400°F / 205°C9–11 minFlip at 5 min
Boneless, 1 inch400°F / 205°C11–14 minMost common size
Boneless, 1 1/2 inch390°F / 199°C14–18 minLower and slower
Bone-in, 1/2 inch400°F / 205°C8–10 minBone slows the center
Bone-in, 3/4 inch400°F / 205°C10–13 minFlip at 5 min
Bone-in, 1 inch390°F / 199°C13–16 minProbe away from bone
Bone-in, 1 1/2 inch390°F / 199°C16–20 minRest 5 min
Breaded, 1/2 inch400°F / 205°C10–12 minPress coating on
Pork loin roast, 2 lb350°F / 177°C35–45 minCheck at 30 min

Bone-in versus boneless

A bone adds flavor and slows heat at the center, so a bone-in chop of the same thickness needs roughly 1–3 minutes more than a boneless one. The bone also confuses thermometers: reading the meat against the bone gives you a high number that has nothing to do with the center. A shallow cut through the fat rim keeps curling bone-in chops flat.

Brining: the fix for dry chops

Pork today is leaner than it was a generation ago, so the window between juicy and dry is narrow. A brine widens it: salt moves into the meat and holds water.

BrineTime in the refrigeratorWhat it does
Dry brine, 1/2 tsp kosher salt per chop40 min to 4 hoursSimplest, and the surface stays dry
Wet brine, 1 tbsp salt per cup of water30 min to 2 hoursFast, but the surface stays wet
Buttermilk brine2–4 hoursMild tang and good browning

Why pork chops dry out

They are lean. Little marbling means nothing bastes the meat from inside as it renders.

They are thin. A 1/2-inch chop passes from done to dry in about 2 minutes.

They keep cooking off the heat. Carryover lifts the center a few degrees after the chop leaves the basket. Pull at 145°F / 63°C, not 155°F / 68°C.

Breaded or plain

Plain chops need a light coat of oil and a hot basket, or a lean chop stays pale. Breaded chops need the opposite: skip the oil in the basket, press a flour, egg and crumb coating firmly onto the meat, and let it brown at 400°F / 205°C. A wet coating that is not pressed on slides off and burns.

Five mistakes with air fryer pork chops

  1. Cooking to 165°F / 74°C. That is the poultry number. Whole cuts of pork are 145°F / 63°C plus a 3 minute rest.
  2. Probing the bone. Bone reads hot. Measure the thickest part of the meat.
  3. Skipping the rest. The 3 minute rest is part of the 145°F / 63°C standard.
  4. Crowding the basket. Two chops touching cook as one thick piece with a cool seam.
  5. Using a thick-chop time on a thin chop. A 1/2-inch chop needs 7–9 minutes.

Frequently asked questions

What temperature do I cook pork chops in an air fryer? 400°F / 205°C up to 1 inch thick, and 390°F / 199°C for thicker chops. In every case the chop must reach 145°F / 63°C and rest 3 minutes before you serve it.

Is 145°F / 63°C safe for pork? Yes, for whole cuts. USDA sets 145°F / 63°C with a 3 minute rest. Ground pork is different: it needs 160°F / 71°C.

Can I put frozen pork chops in the air fryer? Raw frozen chops cook unevenly and are hard to verify, so thaw them first. Breaded frozen chops are made to cook from frozen.

The short version

Set 400°F / 205°C for chops up to 1 inch and 390°F / 199°C for thicker ones, and start checking 2 minutes before the early end of the range. Pull at 145°F / 63°C, rest 3 minutes, and slice against the grain. Ground pork is 160°F / 71°C, not the number on this page.

Always verify doneness with an instant-read thermometer. Cooking times are starting points and vary by appliance model, wattage and basket size.

entry.title: Air Fryer Pork Ribs: Time and Temperature for Tender Racks
entry.summary: Air fryer pork rib times for baby back and spare ribs cut to fit, with the 145°F / 63°C minimum, the foil-wrap method and glaze timing.
entry.content:
Ribs fit an air fryer exactly one way: cut into sections that stand apart in the basket. Cooked that way, they get a bronzed crust and tender meat in under an hour — no smoker, no all-day oven, no charcoal.

Ribs also carry the most confusion in pork cookery: the safe temperature is lower than most people cook them, because ribs are one dish where texture — not safety — decides when they are done.

Times vary by appliance model — use a thermometer. Rack size, cut and glaze change the clock, but the temperatures below do not change.

The temperatures that matter for ribs

Ribs are a whole cut of pork. Under USDA rules, whole cuts of pork are safe at 145°F / 63°C with a three minute rest. That is the floor — and like drumsticks, ribs keep improving well above it as their connective tissue softens:

Doneness stageInternal temperatureResult
USDA minimum for pork145°F / 63°CSafe, but chewy texture
Collagen softening190°F / 88°CTender, pulls from the bone
Fall-off-the-bone203°F / 95°CVery tender, shreddable

Everything at or above 145°F / 63°C is safe. The choice between chewy and fall-off-the-bone is texture, not safety — which is why rib recipes run hotter and longer than the minimum.

Air fryer pork ribs chart

Cut the rack into 3–4 rib sections so air reaches every surface. Remove the membrane from the bone side first — it turns tough and papery otherwise.

RibsTemperatureTimeNotes
Baby back sections, plain rub380°F / 193°C25–32 minTurn at halfway
Baby back, foil-wrapped with liquid350°F / 177°C30–35 minThen unwrap and crisp
Spare rib sections380°F / 193°C32–40 minThicker; check early
Crisp finish, unwrapped400°F / 205°C5–8 minAfter the wrap method

The two-stage method is the most reliable: wrap the sections in foil with a splash of apple juice or water, cook wrapped at 350°F / 177°C for 30–35 minutes to tenderize, then unwrap and finish at 400°F / 205°C for 5–8 minutes to crust. The wrap does the tenderizing; the unwrapped finish does the color.

Glaze timing

Barbecue sauce contains sugar, and sugar scorches above 400°F / 205°C. Sauce during the whole cook and the ribs burn black on the edges. The timing that works:

StepTemperatureTimeNotes
Dry rub only380°F / 193°CFull cookRub builds the base flavor
Sauce in the last 5 minutes380°F / 193°C5 minThin layer, one side at a time
Second sauce layer after cookingOff heatBrush and serveGloss without char

Sauce thin and late. A thick layer applied early insulates the meat and burns before the inside finishes.

Five mistakes with air fryer ribs

  1. Cooking a full rack in one piece. No air gap means steamed middles and burnt edges; cut to fit.
  2. Skipping the membrane removal. The papery layer toughens and blocks seasoning on the bone side.
  3. Saucing from the start. Sugary sauce scorches at high heat; sauce in the last five minutes.
  4. Judging by the minimum. 145°F / 63°C is safe but chewy; ribs are better near 190°F / 88°C.
  5. Cranking past 400°F / 205°C. The glaze burns black before the collagen softens.

Frequently asked questions

How long do ribs take in an air fryer? 25–32 minutes at 380°F / 193°C for baby back sections, turned halfway — or the two-stage method: 30–35 minutes wrapped at 350°F / 177°C, then 5–8 minutes unwrapped at 400°F / 205°C.

What temperature should pork ribs be inside? 145°F / 63°C with a three minute rest is the USDA minimum for pork. Most ribs are better cooked to 190°F / 88°C or above, where the collagen softens and the meat pulls from the bone — safe, just more tender.

Do I need to wrap ribs in foil? For tenderness, yes — the wrap with a splash of liquid braises the meat before the crisp finish. For a chewier, crustier rib, cook unwrapped the whole time.

Can I fit a full rack without cutting it? Only in the largest baskets, coiled into a circle with air in the middle. Cutting into 3–4 rib sections is more reliable and cooks more evenly.

Why are my ribs tough? They stopped below the collagen-softening range. Verify with a thermometer at the thickest section — 145°F / 63°C is safe, but texture needs time near 190°F / 88°C.

Ribs reward the two-stage method: wrapped for tenderness, unwrapped for crust, sauce thin and late. The air fryer turns a rack into dinner in under an hour without lighting anything.

Always verify doneness with an instant-read thermometer. Cooking times are starting points and vary by appliance model, wattage and basket size.

entry.title: Air Fryer Pork Tenderloin: Time and Temperature Guide
entry.summary: Air fryer pork tenderloin times by weight, with the 145°F / 63°C internal rule, carryover cooking and the rest that keeps it juicy.
entry.content:
Pork tenderloin is a lean, boneless cylinder that fits a basket perfectly and roasts in under twenty minutes. It is also one of the easiest proteins to overcook, because there is almost no fat to forgive a mistake — every minute past done shows up as dryness.

The good news is that the target is lower than most people expect. Under USDA rules, whole cuts of pork are safe at 145°F / 63°C with a three minute rest — juicier than the well-done pork of decades past and just as safe.

Times vary by appliance model — use a thermometer. Wattage, basket size and the tenderloin's shape change the clock, but 145°F / 63°C plus rest does not change.

The rule for pork tenderloin

Tenderloin is a whole muscle, not ground meat, so it qualifies for the lower whole-cut standard:

CutSafe internal temperatureRest
Pork tenderloin, whole or medallions145°F / 63°C3 minutes
Pork loin roast, thicker145°F / 63°C3 minutes
Ground pork (not tenderloin)160°F / 71°CNone

Probe the thickest end of the tenderloin — the tail end is always thinner, so it finishes first. Some cooks fold the thin tail under the roast or tuck it beneath to even out the shape; that one move makes the whole piece cook evenly.

Air fryer pork tenderloin chart

Times assume a preheated basket and a whole, untied tenderloin of one to one and a half pounds. Sear-level heat works here because the piece is small and lean.

TenderloinTemperatureTimeNotes
1 lb400°F / 205°C15–18 minNo flipping needed
1.25 lb400°F / 205°C17–20 minCheck at 15 min
1.5 lb400°F / 205°C18–22 minRotate at halfway
Two small tenderloins400°F / 205°C15–18 minSingle layer, air between
Medallions, 1 inch thick400°F / 205°C10–12 minFlip at halfway

Start checking four minutes before the low end of the range. Tenderloin climbs quickly — from 145°F / 63°C to 160°F / 71°C can take only four or five more minutes, and those minutes are the difference between juicy and chalky.

The rest is not optional

The USDA's 145°F / 63°C standard includes a three minute rest, and for good reason: the carryover heat finishes the surface while the juices settle. In practice, a tenderloin pulled at 145°F / 63°C keeps rising during the rest.

Pull from basketTemperature after 5-minute restResult
145°F / 63°CAbout 150°F / 66°CBlush pink center, very juicy
150°F / 66°CAbout 155°F / 68°CBarely pink, firm and juicy
160°F / 71°CAbout 165°F / 74°CWell-done, noticeably drier

All three are safe — the USDA floor is 145°F / 63°C with rest, and anything above it is a texture choice. If you prefer no pink at all, pull at 155°F / 68°C rather than cooking longer in the basket; the rest does the last of the work more gently.

Seasoning that suits a fast roast

Tenderloin takes a dry rub well: salt, pepper, garlic powder, smoked paprika, a pinch of brown sugar. Rub it and let it sit while the basket preheats — twenty minutes at room temperature is enough. Sugary rubs darken quickly at 400°F / 205°C, so keep the sugar small or drop the temperature to 380°F / 193°C and add three to four minutes.

A quick glaze goes on in the last three minutes: honey, mustard and a splash of vinegar, brushed thin. Anything wetter steams the surface instead of glazing it.

Five mistakes with pork tenderloin

  1. Cooking to 160°F / 71°C in the basket. That is well-done territory for a whole cut; pull at 145°F / 63°C and rest.
  2. Skipping the rest. The three minute rest is part of the USDA standard, not a suggestion.
  3. Probing the thin tail. The tail finishes ten minutes early; probe the thick end.
  4. Marinating in sugar from the start. Sweet marinades scorch at 400°F / 205°C before the center is done.
  5. Crowding two tenderloins against the walls. Air must reach every side; leave a gap or cook in batches.

Frequently asked questions

How long does pork tenderloin take in an air fryer? 15–18 minutes at 400°F / 205°C for a one pound tenderloin, 18–22 minutes for one and a half pounds. Check early — the piece cooks fast.

What temperature should pork tenderloin reach? 145°F / 63°C in the thickest part, followed by a three minute rest, per USDA rules for whole cuts of pork. It will stay blush pink inside — that is correct and safe.

Is pink pork safe? At 145°F / 63°C with a proper rest, yes — USDA guidance for whole cuts says exactly that. Ground pork is the exception: it must reach 160°F / 71°C.

Can I cook frozen pork tenderloin? Thaw it first. A frozen tenderloin browns long before the center thaws, which makes an accurate reading impossible. Overnight in the refrigerator is enough.

Why is my tenderloin dry even when cooked right? The piece was larger than the time assumed, or the rest was skipped. Verify with a probe at the thick end and rest five minutes — carryover finishes the job gently.

Lean meat punishes guesswork. Preheat, probe the thick end, pull at 145°F / 63°C, and give the rest its three minutes — the air fryer will return a tenderloin that rivals any oven roast in half the time.

Always verify doneness with an instant-read thermometer. Cooking times are starting points and vary by appliance model, wattage and basket size.

entry.title: Air Fryer Potatoes (Times and Temperatures by Cut)
entry.summary: Air fryer potatoes by cut: wedges, cubes, baby potatoes, slices, hash browns and sweet potatoes, with temperatures, times and the soak-and-dry rule.
entry.content:
Potatoes are the highest-volume air fryer question there is. The difference between a crisp wedge and a pale, limp one is not the machine — it is starch, water and space in the basket.

Times vary by appliance model — use a thermometer for meat and your eyes for potatoes. Wattage, basket size and how full the basket is will move every number below.

The starch rule: soak, then dry completely

Cut potatoes release starch, and that starch is glue. It makes pieces stick together, steams the surfaces that touch, and leaves clumps that are crisp on one side and soft on the other. A 10–30 minute soak in cold water rinses that surface starch off.

Drying matters more. Water on the surface has to evaporate before the potato can brown, so a wet potato steams first and crisps late. Drain, spread the pieces on a towel, and pat them dry.

How much oil

About 1 tablespoon of oil per pound of potatoes — roughly 15 mL per 450 g — and no more than 2 tablespoons for a full 2-pound basket. Toss until every piece has a faint sheen.

More oil does not make crispier potatoes, just greasier ones, and the excess pools in the basket where it burns and smokes. Use a neutral oil with a high smoke point, and finish with butter or olive oil after the basket comes out.

Air fryer potato chart by cut

Times assume a preheated basket, a single layer, and pieces cut to the size named in the row. Add 3–5 minutes if your model runs cool or the basket is more than half full.

Wedges, 3/4 inch thick400°F / 205°C22–26 minShake twice
Cubes, 1 inch400°F / 205°C18–22 minParboil 5 min
Slices, 1/2 inch thick400°F / 205°C16–20 minTurn at halfway
Sliced rounds, 1/4 inch390°F / 199°C12–15 minNo overlap
